proposals.evidence: Platts p. 418 identifies ćāqū “clasp knife, penknife” as Persian. Hindi caku and survey caku/cakku show q adapted as k, with vowel and gemination variation; uncertain intra-IA transfer is retained. Existing Hindi caku “knife” (kannauji[p. 62]) supplies an attested provisional donor. Its locality is the attestation site; the historical lending locality and possible intervening Indo-Aryan language remain unknown. The borrowed edge is saved under the user’s explicit preference to link supported families despite unresolved cross-IA transmission.
